outputs.L1: I am not saying "mark my words," as the thief does early each winter. He leaves nothing of value behind. He, too, wants. A brute possessed of language, he harbors a fondness for preaching. I am bathed to a lustrous sheen. Memories move musically through my bones. He sings above, vaults from a horse with feigned kindness, and lands with such flourish. Releasing all of this, sitting among tropical leaves the size of men within a terrarium, I am beautiful. He means well, admonishing women. He is fortunate in his display of crankiness. What does it mean to relinquish envy? At times I hope the stars refrain from spreading themselves across New York's lights. Performing for himself alone, his glasses glittering, he reads tales of poverty and claims them all as his own. Here in Colorado, irises of every hue unfurl outward toward the half-hidden sun. Upon the cracked cement, chilled before the rain, I perceive perpetual beginnings. I intend to forget him: to lock him in a box within my mind, to lock him in the haunt of violins, to release all that is his in the hurling breath of my groans.
outputs.L2: I won't declare "remember what I tell you," the way the thief does at the start of every winter season. Nothing worthwhile remains after him. He craves things too. This crude creature who wields words takes pleasure in delivering sermons. I've been scrubbed until I shine. Recollections drift like song through my skeleton. He performs overhead, leaps from a horse with false gentleness, and touches down with such style. Releasing all of it, seated among tropical fronds as tall as grown men inside a glass enclosure, I possess beauty. His intentions are good as he scolds women. His displays of irritability serve him well. What is the meaning of releasing this jealousy? Now and then I wish the stars wouldn't scatter themselves across the glow of New York City. Putting on a performance for his own benefit, his spectacles catching the light, he recites tales of the poor and insists every one belongs to him. Out here in Colorado, irises in every shade open toward a sun that's partly concealed. Standing on the fractured pavement, cool with the coming rain, I witness beginnings that never cease. I intend to erase him: seal him inside a container in my mind, confine him where the violins linger, and surrender everything of his through the rush of air in my moaning.

# Letting Go

There is a man who moves through the world like a thief, taking whatever he desires without asking, without apology. He preaches to those around him and admonishes women with a practiced tenderness, feigning kindness even as he reaches for what was never his to claim. His warmth is a costume; beneath it lies only appetite.

He performs, but the performance is always for himself. He gathers up the stories of the poor and the suffering, draping them over his own shoulders as though he had lived them. The pain of others becomes his currency, their hardships a mask he wears to draw sympathy and admiration. Nothing he holds truly belongs to him, yet he speaks as if he had earned it all.

For a long time, I carried envy toward such a man—envy at how easily he took, how confidently he claimed. But I am learning now to set that feeling down. I am searching instead for beauty in the quieter places: in stillness, in memory, in the ordinary miracles of the natural world that ask nothing of me and demand no performance in return.

I think of Colorado, of the irises rising in the spring, of sunlight spilling across the mountains. I think of how each morning offers a perpetual beginning, a fresh chance to start again. These images live in me as symbols of renewal, gentle reminders that hope is always waiting, that the world remakes itself endlessly and invites me to do the same.

And so I resolve to forget this man. I will lock him away in the far rooms of my mind and turn the key. Whatever belongs to him, I release—back into his hands, out of my heart. What is his I no longer need to carry. I am free to keep only what is mine: the stillness, the light, the beginning that waits ahead.
outputs.L4:
# Letting Go: A Reading

The poem unfolds as an intimate reckoning between the speaker and a figure she names only as the "thief"—a character who takes without permission, who appropriates the pain of others and repackages it as his own gospel. This thief does not steal objects but something far more insidious: he claims ownership over suffering that was never his, preaching sermons built from borrowed wounds. Through this recurring figure, the poem establishes a tension between authentic experience and its manipulation, between those who feel deeply and those who perform feeling for their own gain.

The imagery throughout is deliberate and visceral. The thief moves through the verses like a shadow that lengthens and shrinks depending on the light the speaker chooses to shine upon him. At the beginning, he looms large—a preacher on a pulpit constructed from grief, gathering an audience by presenting himself as one who understands anguish, when in truth he has only collected it from others. His theft is spiritual and emotional, a slow erosion of the speaker's sense of what belongs to her. Envy runs beneath his every gesture; he covets what he cannot genuinely possess: the speaker's capacity for real feeling, her resilience, her unguarded heart.

Against this figure, the speaker's own voice begins to emerge and strengthen. Where she once may have surrendered her narrative to his interpretation, she now recognizes the manipulation for what it is. The poem charts this awakening—a gradual reclamation of self that gathers momentum with each stanza. She stops mistaking his preaching for wisdom. She stops allowing her suffering to become material for his performances.

The turning point arrives in the poem's resolution. Rather than continuing to nurse her resentment—which would keep the thief alive within her, feeding him still—the speaker makes a conscious decision to release it. Yet this release is not passive forgetting. In a striking act of imaginative justice, she chooses instead to *mentally imprison* him: to place this figure behind bars of her own construction, contained and rendered powerless, no longer free to roam through her inner life and steal from it.

This dual movement—letting go of resentment while confining the source of harm—becomes the poem's central assertion of liberation. Freed from his grasp, the speaker turns at last toward herself. She affirms her own beauty, not as vanity but as reclamation: a refusal to let another define her worth. In the poem's most resonant phrase, she claims her "perpetual beginnings," embracing the idea that she is never finished, never fixed, never fully taken. She is capable of renewal again and again, of starting fresh no matter what has been stolen before.

Ultimately, the poem stands as a testament to personal liberation. It acknowledges the reality of those who prey upon our pain, but it insists that we hold the final authority over our own stories. Through vivid imagery and an unflinching emotional honesty, the speaker transforms herself from victim to author, from the robbed to the renewed—resolving to move forward whole, beautiful, and endlessly beginning again.
outputs.L5:
# What We Keep, What We Release

There is a strange arithmetic to the human heart. We spend our lives collecting **memories**—gathering them like stones in our pockets, each one weighing something, each one meaning something. But we rarely stop to ask ourselves an important question: **What** are we actually holding onto, and why?

## The Weight of What We Carry

Memories are curious things. They shape who we are, coloring every decision we make and every hope we hold for tomorrow. A childhood afternoon, a first heartbreak, the sound of a loved one's laughter—these moments live inside us long after they have passed. They are proof that we existed, that we felt, that we loved.

Yet not all memories serve us equally. Some warm us like sunlight, while others linger like shadows, keeping us tethered to pain we no longer need to feel.

## The Art of Letting Go

**Letting** go is perhaps one of the hardest skills we ever learn. We fear that releasing a memory means dishonoring it, or that forgetting is a form of betrayal. But letting go is not the same as forgetting.

To let go is to loosen our grip—not on the memory itself, but on the hold it has over us. It means acknowledging what was, honoring what it taught us, and then giving ourselves permission to move forward. Letting go creates space. And in that space, something new can grow.

## What Remains

So **what** truly matters in the end? Perhaps it is not how tightly we cling, but how gracefully we learn to hold things gently.

The best memories don't demand to be gripped—they simply stay, quietly, becoming part of who we are. And the painful ones, when we finally release them, teach us the greatest lesson of all: that we are strong enough to carry what heals us, and wise enough to let go of what does not.

In the end, we are not defined by everything we remember, but by what we choose to keep close—and what we are brave enough to set free.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about letting go of resentment toward a manipulative man, moving between memories and present-day scenes in Colorado and New York.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Mountains Keep**

In Colorado the aspens turn
without asking permission,
gold leaves loosening
one breath at a time.

I used to think forgiveness
was a door I'd open for you—
now I know it's a window
I open for myself.

*Remember the apartment in Queens,*
*how you rearranged the truth*
*like furniture, so I'd trip*
*on my own certainty in the dark?*

You called it love, the way
you'd narrow my world
to the size of your approval,
then blame me for the smallness.

Here the sky is embarrassingly wide.
I hike until my lungs remember
they were never yours to measure.
A hawk writes something illegible
across all that blue
and I don't need to translate it.

*You were good at making me apologize*
*for weather I didn't cause.*
*I carried your storms so long*
*I forgot my own barometric truth.*

In New York I rehearsed my anger
on the 7 train, underground,
a speech for a courtroom
that would never convene.
I wanted you to admit it.
I wanted the sky to crack open.

But resentment is just
a room you keep paying rent on
in a city you've already left.

So today I stop.
I let the aspens teach me
how to release without apology,
how gold is not a loss
but a letting-be.

I don't forgive you
because you've earned it.
I forgive because my hands
are tired of making fists
this far above sea level,
where the air is thin
and I need every breath
for climbing.

Somewhere you are still
rearranging someone's furniture.
Somewhere the 7 train
is still running its dark loop.

But I am here,
where the light comes down
uncomplicated as snowmelt,
and no one—
not even memory—
gets to tell me
this joy is undeserved.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary poem exploring themes of envy, self-worth, and emotional release, using imagery of thieves, winter, irises, and violins.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Thieves Left**

They came in the blue hour, the ones I made
from other people's mornings—
their pockets already full of my sleep,
their hands the color of everything
I wasn't.

I had been counting again.
Her book, his ease, the way
their names arrived in rooms before them
like weather.
I kept my own worth in a jar
and shook it: so little sound.

Winter does this to a person.
It strips the argument down
to the bare grammar of branches,
teaches the field
to hold nothing and call it enough.

Somewhere I read that irises
close their throats at dusk—
not from grief, from economy,
saving the purple for a sun
they trust will come.
I have not learned this trust.
I bloom in the wrong direction,
toward whatever light
is standing in another yard.

But listen—
tonight I took the envy out
and laid it flat as sheet music
on the table.
I did not burn it.
I let it be a thing
with edges I could name.

And a violin somewhere
(a neighbor, a recording, the wind
pretending)
began the slow work
of un-tightening.
That's the secret nobody tells you:
the string must first be loosened
before the true note.

I gave the thieves their bag.
Take the comparisons, I said,
the ledgers, the small cold arithmetic.
Take even the jar.

What's left is snow
melting into the low green
of the first iris,
and my own breath,
finally,
playing itself
like something worth
the hearing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the voice of a woman reclaiming her beauty and peace after being diminished by a self-absorbed, preachy man.
counterfactuals.output:
# What I Kept

You told me I was too much—
my laugh too loud,
my dreams too wide for the small rooms
you kept building around me.

You preached from your paper pulpit,
certain of my flaws,
naming them like scripture
while never once looking up
to see my face.

But I was never yours to shrink.

I have gathered myself back
from the corners where you left me,
swept up the pieces you called broken
and found them only sleeping.

Look—
my shoulders remember how to rise.
My mouth remembers how to sing
without asking permission.

The mirror does not flinch anymore.
It holds me the way morning holds the hills,
unhurried, unashamed,
lit from somewhere you could never reach.

You mistook my silence for agreement.
It was only patience,
the long breath before a woman
decides she is done.

I am not the story you told about me.
I am the one still standing
when the telling ends—

softer where I choose to be soft,
unmovable where it matters,
and beautiful
not because you finally noticed,

but because I stopped
waiting for you to.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental, image-dense poem about forgetting someone and locking them away in memory, blending surreal and natural imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# Cartography of a Sealed Room

I fold you into an envelope of snow
and the snow forgets its own address.

---

There is a door in the back of my skull
where the hinges have grown antlers,
where I hung your voice like a wet coat
and let it drip into the floorboards
until the wood remembered you
better than I could afford to.

*Lock number one:* a river turned to bone.
*Lock number two:* the moth that ate your name
and now wears it, pale and powdery,
against the lamp of my sleeping.

---

I press your face between two pages
of a book written in the language of leaving—
you flatten into a pressed violet,
purple ghost, botanical hush,
a specimen labeled *once, warm.*

The garden in my chest keeps sending up
weeds shaped like your handwriting.
I mow them. They return.
I salt the soil. They bloom in salt.

---

Somewhere a clocktower fills with milk.
Somewhere the hours curdle into a room
I have bricked shut with soft grey stones,
each stone a Sunday we no longer own,
each brick still humming
the frequency of your walking away.

---

Listen:

I have become the keeper of a lighthouse
that shines *inward,*
sweeping its one white blade
across a sea that is only my own held breath.

And you—
you are the ship I keep drawing
smaller and smaller
until you are a pin, a spark, a struck match
dropped into the black water of *enough.*

---

Tonight I turn the final key.
It is made of my own tooth.
It is made of the word I never said.

The door seals.
The antlers bud with frost.
And somewhere, in a house of folded snow,
a coat drips
and drips
and dries.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical poem that begins with the phrase "I am not saying 'mark my words'" and meditates on healing, distance, and inner transformation.
counterfactuals.output:
I am not saying "mark my words"

I am not saying "mark my words,"
as if I held some prophecy,
some certain map of what will come,
some future I could guarantee.

I only mean: I have been walking
longer than I meant to walk,
and something in me learned the quiet
underneath the need to talk.

There was a country made of ache
I lived in for a hundred years—
its rivers ran with all my asking,
its weather was a fog of tears.

I did not leave it in a morning.
Distance is a slower art:
you set one stone, and then another,
across the water of the heart.

And healing does not come like thunder,
loud enior with its light.
It comes the way the dawn arrives—
you cannot name the end of night.

You only notice you are warmer.
You only notice you can breathe.
You only notice that the old grief
loosened, like a coat, its sleeve.

So I am not the one I carried
up those hills of salt and stone.
The distance did its patient sanding.
The waiting made me more my own.

I am not saying "mark my words"—
I am not asking to be right.
I am only saying: I am changed,
and I am walking toward the light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
